description:
We’re a team of mathematicians and gamers working on Be An Earth System Trend Detective. Strong on stats + coding.

Open to new members, especially someone with Earth science, remote sensing, or NASA data experience to strengthen the science side.

We enjoy a relaxed and creative atmosphere, and we also value focused work time where everyone can dig into their part. Happy to discuss ideas when it makes sense, and we like giving each other space to make progress.

Feel free to reach out!
summary:
Terra Whisperers is an interactive tool that lets anyone explore Earth science data and find out whether a change is real. You ask a question in plain words ("Is it getting warmer in Nairobi?"). The app picks the right record among 23 datasets from NASA and its partners, shows it on a globe through time, draws its values for the place, and tests the trend. The answer is one sentence that anyone can read ("Warming, +0.26 °C every 10 years"), with a five-step scale for how sure it is, and it says "no clear trend" when there is none.

It addresses the four objectives of the challenge (select variables, get them for a region, visualise their time series, test whether trends are significant) for people who are not statisticians: farmers and their advisers, communes, teachers, students. It matters because the data is public but out of reach: NASA's catalogue lists more than 50,000 datasets, and reading one takes accounts, portals, file formats and code. Understanding a changing Earth should not take a statistician.
details:
What it does. Terra Whisperers is a web app in the spirit of a digital globe.

- Ask. Terra Explorer reads a question in plain words (English, German, French, Italian, Spanish), chooses the record that fits (the right topic, covering the place and the years, on the finest grid) and says why it chose it and what the record cannot tell.

- See. The variable is drawn on a 3D globe and can be played through time. A place is chosen by a click or by its name; the analysis is for that place or for a square of 50 to 1000 km around it.

- Test. The Trend analysis shows the series, its trend line and a verdict in plain words with a five-step scale ("How sure?"). Behind it: the Mann-Kendall test with the Theil-Sen slope and its confidence interval, allowing for the memory of the record (a year often resembles the one before); the classic Mann-Kendall test and a least-squares line with a t-test are computed beside it. The trend line is carried on for the coming years with its interval, and the app says that this is not a forecast.

- Keep asking. Terra Detective offers 23 ready questions (Has it changed? When did it change? Was this year unusual? What is a normal year here? Where would the past lead?), each answered by checked tools with one sentence, the strength of the evidence and one chart.

How it works. A front end (TypeScript, React, MapLibre GL JS for the globe) and a back end (Python: FastAPI, xarray, Zarr, NumPy, SciPy, pandas) talk through one documented API. Each dataset is stored once as a Zarr store. The globe reads the stores for display; every number in an answer is computed by the back end from the full-precision values, by code covered by 279 automated tests, many of them on made-up data whose answer is known. The data was taken from NASA GISS, NASA POWER, NASA Earthdata (GES DISC, PO.DAAC, LP DAAC), NOAA PSL, the Climate Hazards Center of UC Santa Barbara and MeteoSwiss open data, with import scripts of our own.

What it is good for. A cooperative that asks whether it can still count on the rain, a mountain commune that asks whether winters are warming, a class that wants to see climate change in its own town: each gets a tested answer in a minute, with its limits said in the same sentence. Two cases we worked through: the rain of the growing season at Mopti, Mali (CHIRPS), and winter temperature at Flims, Switzerland (MeteoSwiss, since 1864).

What it does not do. It does not forecast, and it does not explain causes. Monthly means on coarse grids say little about single extreme days, and the app says so where it matters.

Tools and languages. Python 3.12 (FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, xarray, Zarr, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, h5netcdf, earthaccess, pytest, Ruff, uv); TypeScript (React, Vite, zustand, MapLibre GL JS, @carbonplan/zarr-layer); FFmpeg and Playwright for the film; Claude Code (Anthropic) as the AI assistant.
dataRefs: NASA GISTEMP v4, surface temperature change since 1880 (NASA GISS)
https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/
MERRA-2 monthly weather (air temperature, humidity, snow, wind, rain, frost days) and CERES SYN1deg sunshine, through NASA POWER
https://power.larc.nasa.gov/
JPL GRACE and GRACE-FO mascons RL06.3Mv04, water and ice mass (PO.DAAC)
https://doi.org/10.5067/TEMSC-3JC634
MODIS/Terra vegetation indices, monthly, MOD13C2 v061 (LP DAAC)
https://doi.org/10.5067/MODIS/MOD13C2.061
GLDAS Noah 2.1 monthly, root zone soil moisture (GES DISC)
https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/GLDAS_NOAH025_M_2.1/summary
OCO-2 GEOS Level 3 monthly assimilated CO2, v10r (GES DISC)
https://doi.org/10.5067/BGFIODET3HZ8
MERRA-2 M2TMNXSLV v5.12.4, total column ozone (GES DISC)
https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/M2TMNXSLV_5.12.4/summary
NASA Common Metadata Repository (CMR) search API, to find datasets the library does not hold
https://cmr.earthdata.nasa.gov/search/site/docs/search/api.html
NASA Blue Marble imagery and NASA GIBS, for the background of the globe
https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/gibs
NASA Earthdata Login and the `earthaccess` library, to download the Earthdata records
https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov
projectRefs: NOAA ERSST v5 sea surface temperature, GPCP v2.3 rain and snowfall (with NASA), NOAA OI SST v2 sea ice, from NOAA PSL
CHIRPS v3 rainfall, Climate Hazards Center, UC Santa Barbara, with NASA and USGS support
MeteoSwiss open data: temperature and rain since 1864, daily rain reduced to yearly indices of heavy rain, hail days
